flashcards.q: Why does wide-column schema design start from queries, not entities?
flashcards.a: No cheap join and no free secondary access path by default. A query needing differently-shaped data requires a second round trip or write-time denormalization. Design order: enumerate access patterns first, build one table per pattern.

flashcards.q: What is a hot partition and what's the observable symptom?
flashcards.a: A partition key whose cardinality or traffic distribution concentrates rows/requests on one replica set, since all rows sharing a key live together forever. Symptom: one node/replica set at ~100% CPU/IO while the rest of the cluster looks idle; p99 degrades cluster-wide via coordinator overhead.

flashcards.q: Does adding nodes fix a hot partition?
flashcards.a: No, if the cause is key cardinality (not raw capacity) - the hot key still hashes to the same replica set regardless of cluster size. Fix is architectural: salt/shard the partition key and fan out reads.

flashcards.q: State the R+W>N rule and give a strong-consistency and an eventual-consistency example (RF=3).
flashcards.a: R+W>N guarantees every read/write replica set overlaps by >=1 node, so a read sees the latest write. RF=3, W=QUORUM(2), R=QUORUM(2): 2+2=4>3, strong, survives 1 node down. RF=3, W=1, R=1: 1+1=2, not >3, eventual consistency only, fastest.

flashcards.q: Compare STCS, LCS, and TWCS compaction strategies.
flashcards.a: STCS (default): merges similar-size SSTables, can need ~2x disk during large compactions, read amp grows with SSTable count. LCS: fixed-size levels, low read amp but HIGH write amp (repeated rewrites through levels). TWCS: groups SSTables by time window - best for TTL-heavy time-series, expired windows drop predictably.

flashcards.q: What is the tombstone read-latency trap?
flashcards.a: DELETE writes a tombstone, retained until gc_grace_seconds (default 10 days) for replica-repair safety, not removed immediately. A hot-read partition with heavy delete/TTL churn accumulates tombstones the read path scans past, causing timeouts / tombstone_warn/failure_threshold errors - looks like a slow query, is actually scanning graves.

flashcards.q: What is DynamoDB's per-partition physical cap, and what can adaptive capacity NOT do?
flashcards.a: 3,000 RCU/s or 1,000 WCU/s per partition, hard cap. Adaptive capacity smooths moderate/temporary skew up to that cap but cannot raise the physical ceiling - severe sustained skew still throttles.

flashcards.q: LSI vs GSI - the sharpest constraint difference.
flashcards.a: LSI: shares base table partition key, must be declared at table CREATION (can't add later), item collection (base + all LSIs, per partition key) capped at 10GB - hard write failure if exceeded. GSI: own partition key, addable after creation, eventually consistent, own throughput.

flashcards.q: Why can a throttled GSI block writes to a healthy base table?
flashcards.a: DynamoDB propagates writes to GSIs synchronously as part of accepting the base table write, not fully decoupled async - if the GSI's own capacity throttles, the base table write is rejected too, even with spare base table capacity.

flashcards.q: On-demand vs provisioned DynamoDB capacity - when to choose each.
flashcards.a: On-demand: per-request billing, instant elasticity, higher cost/request - safer default for new/unpredictable workloads. Provisioned: pre-declared RCU/WCU (optional auto-scaling with lag), cheaper at steady predictable volume - move here once traffic patterns stabilize.

flashcards.q: Single-table design: what does it buy and what does it cost?
flashcards.a: Buys: fewer round trips per logical op, and under provisioned capacity, one over-provisioning buffer instead of N. Costs: unreadable overloaded generic keys, cross-team schema fragility, hard ad hoc analytics, expensive migrations for unanticipated access patterns.

flashcards.q: When should a team NOT default to single-table design?
flashcards.a: When access patterns are still evolving, when multiple uncoordinated teams share the table, or when ad hoc analytical queries are needed. It assumes fully-enumerated, stable access patterns - most teams should start with simpler per-entity tables.

flashcards.q: How do you fix a hot partition for a time-series IoT table naively keyed by device_id?
flashcards.a: Compound the partition key with a coarser time bucket and/or an entropy suffix, e.g. device_id#2026-08-01#03 (hourly bucket) or device_id#shard_N. Trades a fan-out read (query all shards, merge client-side) for spreading storage and request load across more physical partitions.

flashcards.q: Are DynamoDB and Cassandra interchangeable because both trace to the Dynamo paper?
flashcards.a: No. They have materially different consistency models (Cassandra's per-request tunable R/W consistency vs DynamoDB's simpler eventually-consistent/strongly-consistent read toggle) and different secondary index mechanics (LSI/GSI vs Cassandra secondary indexes/materialized views) and operational models.

flashcards.q: Why is denormalization the default in wide-column modeling, not an optimization applied later?
flashcards.a: Because there's no cheap join, a query needing data shaped differently from storage requires either an extra round trip or duplicating data at write time into a table shaped for that query - you accept write-time duplication and app-managed consistency in exchange for every read being a single-partition operation.
